draft.title: Land degradation
card: Land degradation is a decline in the land's ability to support plants, animals and people. It can come from natural causes, but human activity such as clearing and overgrazing often speeds it up.
Soil erosion
Wind and water remove topsoil, the top layer of soil, which holds most of the nutrients plants need. Bare ground with few plant roots to hold the soil is easily eroded.
Salinity
Salts build up in the soil or near the surface. In many Australian regions, clearing deep-rooted native plants lets the water table rise and bring salts up, which makes it hard for crops to grow.
Loss of vegetation
Removing plant cover takes away food and shelter for animals and exposes the soil. This can lead to more erosion and salinity.
draft.remember: Degradation lowers what the land can support, and losing plant cover can start or worsen it.

a.q: Why does clearing deep-rooted native plants from a slope make soil erosion more likely?
opts: Fewer roots hold the soil, so wind and water remove it
Fewer roots let salts leave the soil, so it dries out
Fewer roots make the soil too rich, so it washes away
Fewer roots stop rain soaking in, so the soil turns salty
a.why: Roots and plant cover hold soil in place. With less cover, wind and water carry topsoil away. Salt is a different problem: it is linked to a rising water table, not to roots holding soil.
a.clue: Think about what plant roots do to the soil around them.

b.q: On a wheat farm in central NSW, cleared paddocks now have white salty patches where crops fail, and the water table has risen. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Clearing deep-rooted plants let the water table rise
Wind removed the topsoil and left the salt behind
Too many crops took the nutrients out of the soil
Heavy rain washed the salts out of the topsoil
b.why: Without deep-rooted plants using the water, the water table rises and brings salts near the surface. Wind erosion is tempting because bare ground is eroded, but the card links salty patches and a rising water table to salinity, not to topsoil being blown away.
b.clue: Look for the option that mentions the water table.

a.best: Fewer roots hold the soil, so wind and water remove it

b.best: Clearing deep-rooted plants let the water table rise

problems.detail: The clue says 'Look for the option that mentions the water table', and only the right option mentions it, so a student can pick the answer without knowing why clearing causes salinity.
The stem already says the water table has risen, and the right option repeats that phrase. Together with the clue, this lets students match words instead of reasoning about the cause.

b.q: On a wheat farm in central NSW, paddocks cleared of native trees decades ago now have white salty patches where crops fail. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The water table rose after clearing and brought salts up
Wind blew the topsoil away and left salt crystals behind
Crops used up the nutrients and left salts in the soil
Rain soaked in and carried salts down to the water table
b.why: The deep-rooted trees used a lot of groundwater. Once they were cleared, the water table rose and carried salts up to the surface. The option about rain carrying salts down is tempting because it also involves the water table, but it has the direction reversed: salinity comes from salts being brought up.
b.clue: What were the cleared trees doing with the water underground?
